question: During rising interest rate environment, most appropriate sector rotation?
before: Rising rates expand bank NIMs (reprice loans faster than deposits). Long-duration growth stocks (IT, tech) suffer from heavier discounting. A partially right but misses bank benefit. B wrong (rate-sensitives hurt). D ignores cycle.
after:
Concept: In a rising interest rate environment, the optimal sector rotation depends on understanding how different business models respond to higher discount rates and credit conditions. Banks benefit from net interest margin (NIM) expansion, while long-duration growth stocks suffer from valuation compression.

Why this is correct: During rising rates, banks can reprice their loan portfolio faster than they need to increase deposit costs, creating a widening spread and higher profitability. Simultaneously, long-duration growth stocks (particularly IT and technology companies with earnings concentrated far in the future) face heavier discounting under higher discount rates, making them less attractive. This combination—overweight banks, underweight long-duration growth—directly captures the dual benefit of the rate cycle.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Overweighting IT and Pharma as defensives misses the core problem: IT earnings are heavily weighted toward distant future years, so higher discount rates compress valuations significantly. Pharma does have some defensive qualities but does not capture the positive NIM expansion story in banks.

B) Overweighting Real Estate and Auto is directly counterintuitive in rising rate environments. Both sectors are highly sensitive to borrowing costs (developers and auto buyers depend on financing), so higher rates increase their cost of capital and suppress demand, hurting profitability.

D) Overweighting all sectors equally ignores the macroeconomic cycle entirely. A mechanical equal-weight approach captures no tactical benefit from rate regime change and forgoes the opportunity to rotate into the strongest performers (banks) while exiting the weakest (long-duration growth).

Intuition: Rising rates create a structural shift in equity attractiveness. Analysts must recognize that the present value of far-future cash flows shrinks sharply, making near-term earnings power (embodied in banks' NIM expansion) far more valuable than growth optionality priced years ahead. This rotation discipline is fundamental to tactical macro positioning in equity portfolios.
